body:
What was the Quit India Movement?

The Quit India Movement was a mass movement against British colonial rule launched by the Indian National Congress under Mahatma Gandhi's leadership in August 1942, during the Second World War. Its central demand was the immediate withdrawal of British rule from India.

The movement is also known as the August Movement or August Kranti. Gandhi wanted Indians to pursue independence through mass nonviolent resistance. However, once the British arrested the principal Congress leaders, the movement developed in different ways across the country, including public demonstrations, underground activities and temporary parallel governments.

Quit India Movement: The nationwide anti-colonial movement launched in August 1942 demanding an immediate end to British rule, with Gandhi's call for determined nonviolent struggle.

The Second World War created a political crisis

The Second World War began in September 1939. Britain involved India in the war without obtaining the consent of India's elected political representatives. Congress leaders objected to India being required to support a war presented as a defence of freedom while India itself remained under colonial rule.

The Indian National Congress was strongly opposed to fascism and Nazism. Its objection was not simply to resisting those forces. Congress argued that an independent India should make its own decisions about participation in the war.

Resignation of Congress ministries

Under the Government of India Act, 1935, elections had been held in 1937, and Congress had formed ministries in several British Indian provinces. These provincial ministries exercised limited self-government while ultimate authority remained with the British.

When Britain refused to accept the Congress demand for a clear commitment to Indian independence after the war, the Congress provincial ministries resigned in 1939. Their resignation demonstrated the growing conflict between colonial wartime control and Indian demands for self-government.

The growing danger from Japan

By 1942, Japan's military advance through Southeast Asia had brought the war close to India's eastern frontier. The fall of British positions in the region weakened confidence in Britain's ability to defend India. Wartime economic difficulties also increased public dissatisfaction.

Gandhi and Congress leaders argued that British withdrawal would enable Indians to organise the defence of their country as a free people. Thus, the demand for independence became closely connected with the international wartime situation.

Why the Cripps Mission failed

In March 1942, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India to seek Indian political cooperation with the Allied war effort.

The proposals offered a framework for Indian self-government after the war. They included the creation of a constitution-making body after hostilities ended and the possibility of a new Indian Union enjoying Dominion Status. Dominion Status meant self-government within a constitutional relationship with the British Commonwealth, rather than the immediate ending of all British authority in India.

Congress rejected the proposals because they did not provide an immediate transfer of effective power. The continuation of British control over defence during the war and the provision allowing provinces to remain outside the proposed Indian Union were important objections.

Cripps Mission versus Quit India: The Cripps proposals concerned arrangements for self-government after the war. The Quit India demand, made later in 1942, insisted that British rule must end immediately.

The failure of negotiations strengthened the belief among Congress leaders that further requests for constitutional concessions would not secure immediate freedom. This provided the direct political background to the Quit India resolution.

Prelims focus

  • The Quit India Movement began in August 1942, during the Second World War.
  • Congress provincial ministries resigned in 1939 over Britain's wartime policy and refusal to meet the demand for independence.
  • Sir Stafford Cripps led the Cripps Mission in 1942.
  • The Cripps proposals offered a postwar constitutional settlement, not immediate independence.
  • Trap: Congress opposition to British colonial rule did not mean that Congress supported Japanese expansion or fascism.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed pp. 122–123; British Government, 'Cripps Proposals: Text of Constitutional Proposals', 1942, clauses concerning the proposed Indian Union and constitution-making body, reproduced in Ministry of External Affairs documentary records; The National Archives, United Kingdom, 'Indian Independence, Part One', Source 5: Cripps, Nehru and Gandhi (consulted 21 November 2026); Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, 'Quit India, 1942', sections on the Cripps Mission and the Quit India resolution (consulted 21 November 2026).]

title: Why the Quit India Movement Began in 1942

body:
From the Wardha decision to the Bombay session

Following the failure of the Cripps Mission, the Indian National Congress moved towards a mass struggle. On 14 July 1942, the Congress Working Committee met at Wardha and approved a resolution calling for an immediate end to British rule.

The Congress Working Committee was the principal executive decision-making body of the party. Its July decision prepared the ground for consideration by the wider All India Congress Committee (AICC).

On 8 August 1942, the AICC adopted the historic Quit India Resolution at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, now Mumbai. The site is known today as August Kranti Maidan.

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was the Congress president at the time. Mahatma Gandhi provided the principal moral and political leadership of the movement, while other prominent Congress leaders, including Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, supported the struggle.

What did the resolution demand?

The resolution declared that the immediate end of British rule was necessary both for India's freedom and for the wider struggle against aggression and imperialism during the war.

Its basic demand was straightforward: Britain should transfer political authority so that Indians could govern and defend their country themselves. The Congress proposed a mass struggle if this demand was not accepted.

Gandhi's message: Do or Die

At the Bombay meeting, Gandhi gave the call Do or Die. It expressed the determination to secure independence rather than accept the indefinite continuation of colonial rule.

Gandhi's instruction was tied to ahimsa, or nonviolence. He expected people to resist colonial authority through peaceful mass action, even if that required accepting imprisonment and other hardships.

Two slogans, two associations: The expression Quit India was suggested by nationalist leader Yusuf Meherally. The famous call Do or Die was given by Mahatma Gandhi during the Bombay session.

9 August 1942: British arrests and the public response

The British government acted almost immediately. In the early hours of 9 August 1942, Gandhi and leading Congress figures, including Nehru, Patel and Azad, were arrested.

Gandhi was detained at the Aga Khan Palace in Pune. Several members of the Congress Working Committee were held at Ahmednagar Fort. Congress organisations were declared unlawful, their offices were subjected to restrictions, and further arrests followed.

The government intended to prevent an organised nationwide campaign by removing its senior leadership before the struggle could develop. Instead, the arrests provoked widespread anger and encouraged local groups to act on their own initiative.

Aruna Asaf Ali and the flag at Gowalia Tank

On 9 August 1942, Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the national flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan despite government restrictions. Her action became a symbol of continued resistance after the arrest of the senior Congress leaders.

The event illustrates an important feature of Quit India: although Gandhi and the Congress leadership had initiated the movement, ordinary participants and leaders who remained outside prison continued it without sustained direction from the central leadership.

Prelims focus

  • 14 July 1942: Congress Working Committee decision at Wardha.
  • 8 August 1942: Quit India Resolution adopted by the AICC at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay.
  • 9 August 1942: Gandhi and other senior Congress leaders arrested.
  • 9 August 1942: Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank.
  • Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was the Congress president; Gandhi gave the Do or Die call.
  • Trap: The resolution was adopted on 8 August; the major leadership arrests occurred on 9 August.

[Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, 'Quit India, 1942', sections 'Quit India Resolution' and the events of 9 August (consulted 21 November 2026); Jawaharlal Nehru, 'Quit India Resolution', Working Committee draft dated 5 August 1942, reproduced in Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, First Series, Vol. 12, pp. 436–453, The Nehru Archive (consulted 21 November 2026); Employment News, Vol. 18, 4–10 August 2018, 'Quit India Movement: An Important Milestone in Our Struggle for Freedom'; Lok Sabha Secretariat, The Journal of Parliamentary Information, December 1992, 'Addresses at the Celebration of the 50th Anniversary of the Quit India Movement', p. 447.]

title: The Quit India Resolution, Gandhi's Call and the Arrests of August 1942

body:
Why Quit India became a mass movement

The arrest of the senior Congress leadership did not end the movement. On the contrary, protests spread rapidly to towns, villages and districts across India.

The movement is described as a mass movement because participation extended well beyond established political leaders. Students, peasants, workers, women and local volunteers entered the struggle in large numbers. They protested against British rule through public meetings, processions, strikes and other forms of resistance.

Participation was widespread but not equally intense in every region. Local political organisation, public grievances and the severity of government repression influenced how the movement developed.

How different groups participated

Students and young people

Students left schools and colleges to join demonstrations, organise processions and circulate nationalist information. Some later helped underground networks when open political activity became dangerous.

Peasants and rural communities

In rural districts, peasants joined protests and challenged symbols of colonial administration. In some places, crowds attacked police stations or other government establishments. Rural participation helped the agitation spread beyond major cities.

Industrial workers

Workers joined strikes and shutdowns, especially in centres where nationalist activity already had a strong base. A strike or hartal involved a temporary stoppage of work or commercial activity to express political protest.

Women participants

Women joined demonstrations, carried messages, organised resistance and took leadership roles. Their contribution was not confined to supporting male leaders. Aruna Asaf Ali became prominent in public and underground activity, while Matangini Hazra was killed by police firing while leading a protest procession in the Tamluk area of Bengal in September 1942.

From public protest to attacks on colonial authority

Early reactions included peaceful processions, meetings and hartals. As police restrictions and repression intensified, some demonstrations developed into confrontations.

In several areas, protesters damaged railway lines, telegraph and telephone facilities, police stations and other government property. Railway and telegraph systems were particularly important to colonial administration because they allowed officials to transport personnel and communicate orders.

Disrupting these facilities was intended to weaken the ability of the colonial government to exercise control. Such actions were different from Gandhi's stated programme of nonviolent resistance.

Do not confuse Gandhi's instructions with every action of the movement. Gandhi advocated nonviolence. However, the actual uprising included both peaceful resistance and acts of sabotage or violence, especially after the rapid arrest of national leaders and the use of force against demonstrators.

Major areas of participation

Strong agitation occurred in parts of Bihar, eastern United Provinces, Bengal, Maharashtra and coastal Odisha. Important centres included Ballia, Midnapore and Satara. Nationalist activity also occurred in Gujarat, including Ahmedabad and the Bharuch region.

Gujarat: student participation in Ahmedabad

In Ahmedabad, students participated actively in the August 1942 protests. Vinod Kinariwala, a student associated with Gujarat College, was killed in police firing during an anti-British student gathering on 10 August 1942.

His death illustrates both the role of students in the movement and the severe response of the colonial authorities. A memorial to Vinod Kinariwala stands at Gujarat College in Ahmedabad.

Prelims focus

  • Students, peasants, workers and women were important participants in the Quit India Movement.
  • Hartals were strikes or shutdowns used to express political protest.
  • Railway lines, telegraph facilities and government establishments were attacked in some areas.
  • Vinod Kinariwala was killed during student protests at Gujarat College, Ahmedabad, on 10 August 1942.
  • Matangini Hazra is associated with the 1942 movement in the Tamluk area of Bengal.
  • Trap: The movement included violent incidents, but Gandhi's stated method remained nonviolent struggle.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed p. 123; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement', section 'Quit India', printed p. 363; Employment News, Vol. 18, 4–10 August 2018, 'Quit India Movement: An Important Milestone in Our Struggle for Freedom', sections on the spread and forms of protest; Indian Council of Historical Research and Ministry of Culture, Dictionary of Martyrs: India's Freedom Struggle, Vol. 3, first edition 2014, entry 'Vinod Kinariwala', printed p. 293; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, 'Gujarat College' (consulted 21 November 2026); Press Information Bureau, 'Quit India Movement', 5 August 2017 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Different social groups joined the movement through different forms of action.
